studyPages.title: What Is Fire
studyPages.body:
WHAT IS FIRE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what what is fire means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show what is fire.
• Correct one common mistake about what is fire.

INTRODUCTION
----
Quick question: how would you explain What Is Fire — Combustion basics for Grade 8 to a classmate in one minute? Anchor answer: Combustion basics for Grade 8. Clue from real life: Fires can be classified between four and seven classes. Check every example on this page against that anchor.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Fires can be classified between four and seven classes.
• The following are six classes of fire mostly widely used and accepted.
• Fires that burn materials such as wood, cloth, paper and plastics.
• Fires that involve liquids such as grease, oils, paraffin, petrol, diesel and alcohol.
• Fires that involve gases such as propane, butane and methane.
• Fires that are ignited by combustible metals such as potassium, sodium, aluminium and magnesium.
• These fires are ignited by cooking oil and animal fats.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
Worked situation (a hardware shop in Nakuru): a learner investigates what is fire. First observation: Fires can be classified between four and seven classes. Because of that observation, the learner names the correct scientific idea and rejects a near-miss confusion. So the conclusion is written in one accurate sentence that matches the main notes — with the correct symbol or formula if one applies (H₂O, NaCl, Fe, P = F / A).

IN EVERYDAY LIFE
----
At a hardware shop in Nakuru, what is fire shows up when you handle real materials or processes linked to this idea. Safety tip: protect your eyes when heating and never taste unknown chemicals.

SUMMARY
----
• Fires can be classified between four and seven classes.
• The following are six classes of fire mostly widely used and accepted.
• Fires that burn materials such as wood, cloth, paper and plastics.
• Fires that involve liquids such as grease, oils, paraffin, petrol, diesel and alcohol.

studyPages.title: The Fire Triangle
studyPages.body:
THE FIRE TRIANGLE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what the fire triangle means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show the fire triangle.
• Correct one common mistake about the fire triangle.

INTRODUCTION
----
A candle goes out when you cover it with a jar — not because the wax disappeared, but because oxygen was cut off. Fire needs fuel, heat and oxygen together. Remove any one side of that triangle and burning stops.

MAIN NOTES
----
• A fire needs three things at the same time: fuel, heat, and oxygen. Together they form the fire triangle.
• Fuel is anything that can burn, such as wood, paper, petrol, or cooking oil.
• Heat raises the fuel to its ignition temperature.
• Oxygen from the air supports burning. If you remove any one side of the triangle, the fire can go out.

WORKED EXAMPLE
----
At a market stall near a kitchen in Kisumu, cooking oil on a cloth catches fire.
First identify the three parts present: fuel (oil/cloth), heat (flame), oxygen (air).
Because all three are present, the fire continues.
Owino reaches for water — wrong for an oil fire, because water can spread the burning fuel.
Correct action: cut oxygen/heat safely with a cover and move people away — removing one side of the triangle.

• Fuel is anything that can burn, such as wood, paper, petrol, or cooking oil.
• Heat raises the fuel to its ignition temperature.
• Oxygen from the air supports burning. If you remove any one side of the triangle, the fire can go out.

studyPages.title: Removing Fuel from a Fire
studyPages.body:
REMOVING FUEL FROM A FIRE
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what removing fuel from a fire means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show removing fuel from a fire.
• Correct one common mistake about removing fuel from a fire.

INTRODUCTION
----
Turn off the gas on a stove and a small kitchen flame often dies — you removed the fuel supply. Starving a fire of fuel is one way to break the fire triangle, used carefully with adult or teacher guidance.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Helps us to remove sources of ignition (sparks, smoking, flames or hot surfaces) when working with flammable and combustible products.
• This will help to prevent the fire from starting and spreading.
• A water fire extinguisher would be the safest way of doing this.
• However, these extinguishers cannot be used on all types of fire.\.
• This can be achieved by using either a carbon (IV) oxide or a form fire extinguisher.
• Fire extinguisher come in different types depending on the kind of environment you are in. Some places such as school, work or home, one or more types of fire extinguishers may be required.
• The following are different types of fire extinguishers and the classes of fire they put.

====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what removing heat from a fire means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show removing heat from a fire.
• Correct one common mistake about removing heat from a fire.

INTRODUCTION
----
Cooling hot embers with water removes heat energy the fire needs to keep going. That is why water works on many Class A fires: it lowers temperature below what the fuel needs to keep burning.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Fire hose is a highpressure pipe used to carry water or retardant.
• Dangerous for classes E and F.
• Carbon (IV) oxide fire extinguisher.
• Dangerous for classes A and C.

• Wet chemical fire extinguisher.
• Dangerous for class B, C, D and E.

studyPages.body:
WHY WATER IS NOT UNIVERSAL
====

WHAT YOU WILL LEARN
----
• Say what why water is not universal means in plain words.
• Use one real Kenyan example to show why water is not universal.
• Correct one common mistake about why water is not universal.

INTRODUCTION
----
Water puts out many wood fires, so learners assume it works on every fire. That assumption is dangerous. On petrol or electrical fires, water can spread fuel or conduct current — so matching the method to the fire class is the real skill.

MAIN NOTES
----
• Dangerous for classes E and F.
• Dangerous for classes A and C.
• Wet chemical fire extinguisher.

WORKED EXAMPLE
